title: Fix Your Curriculum Resources First! (But Not in the Way You Think)
author: Ollie Lovell
summary: Responding to a question Craig Barton posed after an earlier EdThread post, Ollie Lovell clarifies what he means by 'fixing' curriculum resources early in a school-improvement journey. He distinguishes two meanings of 'fix': making resources state-of-the-art, which he does not advocate rushing, versus prescribing, sharing, and setting resources in place as a shared starting point, which he does advocate early. Without a concrete, shared set of worked examples, student work samples, and assessments, Lovell argues departments end up talking in vague generalities, and those unstated differences quietly shape student learning outcomes regardless. His conclusion: fixing resources in place isn't the finish line for improvement, but it is the necessary concrete starting point from which genuine, iterative improvement can actually happen.
points: Lovell distinguishes two senses of 'fix': making resources state-of-the-art (not his recommendation to rush) versus prescribing and sharing a concrete, shared starting point (his actual recommendation, early in an improvement journey).

His core argument: without shared, prescribed resources, departments talk in vague generalities -- a 'worked example' means something different to each teacher -- even though the exact resources chosen have 'enormous impacts on student learning.'

He frames fixed curriculum resources not as the endpoint of school improvement but as the concrete bedrock from which iterative improvement can happen in parallel with other priorities like behaviour and formative assessment.
He explicitly clarifies a prior post after Barton's own pushback, showing the exchange directly shaped how Lovell articulated the argument.
quotes: In no way do I think that schools should 'fix' their curriculum resources before any other improvement initiative if by 'fix' we mean, 'make state-of-the-art'.
But I do think that schools should 'fix' their curriculum resources at a relatively early stage of an improvement journey where to 'fix' means to 'prescribe, share, and set in place'.

Without curriculum resources fixed in place, teachers end up speaking in generalities. A department member might say, ‘I taught that with a worked example’, ignoring the fact that every other teacher in the department has a different understanding of what that term, ‘worked example’, means.
The point is not to get it completely right the first time, the point is to have a concrete starting point from which to improve.
Having prescriptive and shared curriculum resources is one of the ingredients of high performing schools. Without it, we're adrift in a world world of ambiguity.
